read.sections.0.heading.source: Art that does not last, memory that does
read.sections.0.heading.back: Art that does not last long, but memory that lasts long

read.sections.0.text.source:
An artwork does not have to last for centuries to matter. Flowers, food, paper and short-lived structures can bring people together around a shared memory. In Mexico, Día de Muertos, or Day of the Dead, joins artistic making with remembering people after their death. Its meanings belong to living communities, whose practices keep changing.

UNESCO recognises the festival as practised by Mexico's Indigenous communities. It lists it as intangible heritage: knowledge and practices passed between people. UNESCO's account describes celebrations in late October and early November. This is near the end of the season when maize grows. For people who hold this belief, relatives who have died return for a short time. Families prepare favourite foods. They arrange flowers, candles and paper decorations. These actions keep up bonds between generations. They help people feel part of a community. You can study this belief without sharing it.
read.sections.0.text.note: Sensitive lesson (death, grief, belief). Beliefs are framed as beliefs (สำหรับผู้ที่มีความเชื่อนี้ / บางคนเชื่อว่า); 'favourite foods' as อาหารที่ญาติเหล่านั้นชอบ (โปรด avoided). Indigenous as ชนพื้นเมือง.
read.sections.0.text.back:
An artwork does not need to last for centuries to matter. Flowers, food, paper and structures that last only a short time can bring people together around shared memory. In Mexico, the Day of the Dead, or Día de Muertos, combines making art with remembering people after they have died. The meaning of this day belongs to living communities, whose practices keep changing all the time.

UNESCO recognised this festival in the form practised by Mexico's Indigenous communities and inscribed it as intangible cultural heritage, that is, knowledge and practices passed on between people. UNESCO's description mentions celebrations in late October and early November, near the end of the maize-growing season. For those who hold this belief, relatives who have died return for a short time. Families prepare foods those relatives liked and arrange flowers, candles and decorations made of paper. These actions keep the bonds between generations and help people feel part of a community. You can study this belief without needing to believe it.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
Art does not have to last to matter. Flowers, food and paper can bring people together to remember. In Mexico, Día de Muertos means Day of the Dead. People make art to keep the dead in mind. It belongs to living people, and it keeps changing.

UNESCO says Indigenous groups in Mexico practise it. It calls it intangible heritage. That means skills and ways that people pass on. It comes in late October and early November. That is when the maize, or corn, season ends. Some people believe that relatives who have died come back for a short time. Families cook the foods these relatives liked. They set out flowers, candles and paper. This links old and young. It helps them feel they belong. You can learn about a belief and not share it.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
Art does not need to last long to matter. Flowers, food and paper can help people come together and remember together. In Mexico there is a day called Día de Muertos, which means the Day of the Dead. People make art to remember those who have passed away. This day belongs to the people who are still living, and it keeps changing.

UNESCO says Indigenous groups in Mexico practise this. UNESCO calls this intangible cultural heritage, meaning skills and ways that people pass on. This day is in late October and early November, the time when the maize season ends. Some people believe relatives who have died come back for a short time. Families make food these relatives liked. They lay out flowers, candles and paper. This connects older and younger generations and helps them feel they belong. You can learn about a belief without believing it.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Histories of change, many local forms
read.sections.1.heading.back: A history of change, and many local forms

read.sections.1.text.source:
These practices have histories of change. In the sixteenth century, Europeans brought Catholic feasts to Mexico. Indigenous religious traditions became linked with them. All Saints' Day falls on 1 November, and All Souls' Day on 2 November. Religious images and older practices could take on meanings together. But not every Indigenous people, Mexican family or Catholic community celebrates in the same way. Place, family traditions and beliefs shape different forms.

For example, in the Huasteca region the festival is called Xantolo. It includes processions, or walking parades, with masked performers called Huehues. UNESCO's account says that costumes, music and characters differ from one community to the next. So a national festival name holds many local histories. A public museum display also has a different setting and audience from an ofrenda in a family home. An ofrenda is an offering. The word also means the arranged altar or display of offerings.
read.sections.1.text.note: Names in Thai letters: Huasteca ภูมิภาคฮัวสเตกา, Xantolo ซานโตโล, Huehues เวเวส, Coyoacán โกโยอากัน, Mexico City เม็กซิโกซิตี. José Guadalupe Posada (a person) and Día de Muertos (given with its Thai meaning วันแห่งความตาย) stay in Latin letters. Catholic feast names follow Thai Catholic usage as I understand it: วันสมโภชนักบุญทั้งหลาย (All Saints) and วันระลึกถึงผู้ล่วงลับ (All Souls); a Catholic reviewer should confirm.
read.sections.1.text.back:
These practices have a history of change. In the 16th century CE, Europeans brought Catholic feasts to Mexico, so Indigenous religious traditions became connected with those feasts. All Saints' Day falls on 1 November and All Souls' Day on 2 November. Religious images and older practices can share meanings, but not every Indigenous group, every Mexican family or every Catholic community celebrates in the same way. Place, family traditions and beliefs produce different forms.

For example, in the Huasteca region the festival is called Xantolo. There are processions, or walking in a line, with masked performers called Huehues. UNESCO's description says costumes, music and characters differ from community to community. So one national festival name holds many local histories inside it. A display in a public museum also has a different setting and audience from an ofrenda in a family's home. An ofrenda is an offering; the word also means the altar or display of offerings that has been arranged.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
These ways have changed. In the 1500s, Europeans brought Catholic feast days to Mexico. Old Indigenous ways became linked with them. All Saints' Day is on 1 November, and All Souls' Day on 2 November. Old ways and Catholic images came to share meanings. But not every family or group does the same. Place, family and belief make each one its own.

In the Huasteca region, the festival is called Xantolo. People walk in a line, with masked performers called Huehues. UNESCO says the clothes, music and roles differ from group to group. So one name holds many local stories. An ofrenda is an offering. It is also the altar where offerings are set out. A museum ofrenda is for the public. It differs from one in a home.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
These ways changed over time. In the years 1500 to 1599, Europeans brought Catholic feast days to Mexico. So the old Indigenous ways became connected with those feast days. All Saints' Day falls on 1 November and All Souls' Day on 2 November. So the old ways and Catholic images share meanings. But not every family or every group does the same thing. Place, family and beliefs give each place its own form.

In the Huasteca region, this festival is called Xantolo. People walk in a line with masked performers called Huehues. UNESCO says the clothes, music and roles differ from group to group. So one name holds many local stories. An ofrenda is an offering, and also an altar where offerings are laid out. An ofrenda in a museum is set up for the general public to see, so it is different from an ofrenda at home.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Paper, arrangement and a printed skeleton
read.sections.2.heading.back: Paper, arrangement and the skeleton in the print

read.sections.2.text.source:
An ofrenda gives memory a shape people can see. Photographs, food, flowers and other objects can show who is being remembered. They also make the space welcoming. The museum example in the photograph is in Coyoacán, in Mexico City. It has stepped levels, bright paper decoration and model skeleton figures. Its file record says it is dedicated to the Virgin of Guadalupe. This display brings Catholic images and festive making together in one public space. It cannot stand for every household altar.

Papel picado, paper with cut-out designs, needs knowledge of pattern and material. Makers cut designs into thin tissue paper and join the sheets into banners. Skilled artisans can cut several layers at once, repeating a design. The paper may not last long, but the knowledge of making it continues. Setting up a short-lived altar also takes planning, choices and work. The finished photograph shows only part of this.

Printed images have also changed how the festival looks in public. José Guadalupe Posada's Calavera Catrina shows a skeleton wearing a grand hat. A calavera is a skull, or an artistic image of a skull or skeleton. Posada's skeleton pictures used satire: humour that criticises behaviour or power. Later artists helped make his image widely known. Its later link with Día de Muertos is one chapter in a longer history. Posada did not invent the older celebration. Together, the print and the museum ofrenda show how old practices, new art and changing audiences can keep a tradition alive.
read.sections.2.text.note: satire as การเสียดสี; papel picado banners as ธงราว; relief print (captions) as ภาพพิมพ์ผิวนูน. Check.
read.sections.2.text.back:
An ofrenda gives memory a shape people can see. Photographs, food, flowers and other objects can tell who is being remembered, and also make the space look warm and welcoming. The museum example in the photograph is in Coyoacán in Mexico City, with stepped tiers, brightly coloured paper decorations and skeleton figures. The image file's record says the display is dedicated to Our Lady of Guadalupe. This display brings Catholic religious imagery together with creative festival work in one public space, but it cannot represent every home altar.

Papel picado, paper cut out into patterns, requires knowledge of patterns and materials. Craftspeople cut patterns into thin paper, then join the sheets into strings of flags. Skilled artisans can cut many layers of paper at once to get repeated patterns. The paper may not last long, but the knowledge of making it carries on. Arranging an altar that does not last long also needs planning, choosing and effort. A photograph of the finished work shows only part of these things.

Prints also changed the festival's public look. José Guadalupe Posada's “Calavera Catrina” shows a skeleton wearing a large, fancy hat. A calavera is a skull, or an artistic image of a skull or skeleton. Posada's skeleton pictures used satire, humour that criticises behaviour or power. Later artists helped make his image widely known. This image's later connection with the Day of the Dead is only one chapter in a longer history. Posada did not invent the older celebration. Together, the print and the museum ofrenda show how old practices, new art and changing audiences help a tradition stay alive.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
An ofrenda puts memory into a shape you can see. Photos, food and flowers can show who is remembered. They make the space feel welcoming. The photo shows a museum ofrenda in Mexico City. It has steps, bright paper and model skeletons. Its record says it is for the Virgin of Guadalupe. But one display cannot stand for every home altar.

Papel picado is paper with cut-out designs. Makers cut patterns into thin paper. They join the sheets into long banners. Skilled makers can cut many sheets at once. The paper does not last long. But the skill to make it lives on. A photo shows just part of the work.

Prints also changed how the day looks. The artist José Guadalupe Posada made a print called Calavera Catrina. A calavera is a skull, or a picture of a skull or skeleton. His skeleton wears a big, fancy hat. Posada used satire. Satire is humour that makes fun of how people act, or of power. Later artists made his picture famous. Now people link it with this day. But Posada did not invent the day. It is much older. Old ways, new art and new viewers keep it alive.
read.sections.2.simpler.back:
An ofrenda gives memory a shape we can see. Photographs, food and flowers can tell who is being remembered. These things make the space look warm. The photograph shows an ofrenda in a museum in Mexico City, with steps, bright paper and skeleton figures. The record says it was set up for Our Lady of Guadalupe. But one display cannot represent every home altar.

Papel picado is paper cut into patterns. Craftspeople cut patterns into thin paper, then join the sheets into long strings of flags. Skilled craftspeople can cut many sheets at once. The paper does not last long, but the skill of making it carries on. The photograph shows only part of the work.

Prints also changed how this day looks. An artist named José Guadalupe Posada made a print called “Calavera Catrina”. A calavera is a skull, or a picture of a skull or skeleton. His skeleton wears a large, fancy hat. Posada used satire. Satire is humour that makes fun of what people do, or makes fun of power. Later artists made his picture famous. Now people connect this picture with the Day of the Dead, but Posada did not invent this day. This day is much older than that. Old ways, new art and new audiences help this day stay alive.

A carpet of flowers and fruit lies on the floor in front. Life-size dressed skeleton models stand on both sides.

On the floor in front is a carpet made of flowers and fruit, and on both sides stand life-size clothed skeleton figures.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: This lesson is about death and remembrance, and some learners may be grieving, including after losses linked to displacement. No one is asked to share about people they have lost, to describe a death, or to perform or take part in any practice. Don't ask for a bereavement example: the Write task uses only the photograph and the reading.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: This lesson is about death and remembering those who have passed away. Some learners may be grieving, including losses connected with being displaced. Nobody is asked to tell about someone they lost, describe a death, or do or join any ritual. Do not ask learners to give examples of loss. The Write task uses only the photograph and the reading.

sensitiveNotes.1.source: Describe beliefs as beliefs, and teach the communities as present-day makers and decision-makers. No learner is asked to share their religion. Avoid presenting the festival as an unchanged survival, a Mexican version of Halloween, or a tradition invented by Posada.

sensitiveNotes.2.source: Both pictures were inspected for the brief: the print is an artistic skeleton and the photograph shows model skeletons in a public display, not human remains. Neither shows gore, mourners or a funeral.
sensitiveNotes.2.back: Both images have been checked against the requirements. The print is a skeleton in an artwork, and the photograph shows skeleton figures in a public display, not human remains. No image shows bloody violence, mourners or a funeral.

educatorNotes.0.source: UNESCO's inscription concerns Indigenous practices; it is not a claim that all Mexicans observe one uniform festival. Don't assign a meaning to each object or level without evidence for that particular community. Allow about 15 minutes for the reading and pictures, 10–15 for the short responses and 5 for reflection.
educatorNotes.0.back: UNESCO's inscription is about Indigenous practices and does not claim all Mexicans celebrate the same festival in the same way. Do not assign meanings to individual objects or tiers without evidence from the community concerned. Allow about 15 minutes for the reading and pictures, 10–15 minutes for short answers and 5 minutes for reflection.

educatorNotes.1.source: Answer points for Write: a supported link between the arranged objects (paper, flowers, levels) and remembering, making or sharing meaning with an audience, recognising this as one public museum example. Accept continuity through learned skills, or change through new imagery. Don't infer a particular person being remembered from this Guadalupe-dedicated public display, and don't require a personal religious statement.
educatorNotes.1.back: Answer points for the Write step: an evidence-supported connection between the arranged objects (paper, flowers, tiers) and remembering, creating or sharing meaning with an audience, recognising that this is one example from a public museum. Accept answers about continuity through learned skills or change through new kinds of images. Do not assume any particular person is being remembered from this public display dedicated to Our Lady of Guadalupe, and do not make learners express their religious beliefs.

educatorNotes.2.source: Source limits: Norma Cantú's family recollections are particular experiences, not universal rules. The Lam Museum's papel picado and Catrina pages support the paper-making and the print's later popularity; ignore the Catrina page's conflicting birth-year details and keep the Amon Carter's date and attribution. The Carter print is not the origin of the older festivities, and the photograph's record does not name the display's makers.
educatorNotes.2.back: Source limits: Norma Cantú's family memories are a personal experience, not a rule that applies to everyone. The Lam Museum's web pages on papel picado and the Catrina support information about paper-making and the print's later popularity. Ignore the conflicting birth-year details on the Catrina page and use the Amon Carter's date and attribution. The Amon Carter print is not the origin of the older festival, and the photograph's record does not name who made the display.
